newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALGERIA'S ZEROUAL CLAIMS VICTORY OVER GUERRILLAS.
newsitem.headline: ALGERIA'S ZEROUAL CLAIMS VICTORY OVER GUERRILLAS.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual, addressing a rally a month before parliamentary elections, said on Saturday his government had defeated Moslem rebels.

"The terrorism in our country has lost the war thanks to the courage and sacrifices of our people and its security forces," Zeroual told the gathering in the town of Ghardaia, 470 km (290 miles) south of Algiers.

Algerian officials use the term "terrorism" to refer to actions of Moslem guerrillas who took up arms to topple the government after army-backed authorities in 1992 cancelled general elections in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
About 60,000 people have been killed in political violence since then and the bloodshed has continued despite repeated government claims of victory over the rebels.

Zeroual, whose speech was broadcast by state-run radio, said the rebels "are criminals who have no relation with the people and with the Moslem faith. They are criminals who cut the throats of babies, women and innocent citizens."
"The state respects its commitment to exterminate those criminals and treacherous who are taking their revenge on the people by slaugtering innocent people," he vowed.
Suspected Moslem rebels killed more than 300 people, most of them villagers, in an upsurge of violence in April.

"The state has the firm determination to restore peace and stability in the country," said Zeroual, who was appointed head of state in 1994 and won Algeria's first multi-candidate presidential election in November 1995.
Zeroual said the June 5 parliamentary elections would be another "political victory" on the path to establish multi-party democracy in Algeria. Local elections would be held soon afterwards, he said.

About 8,000 candidates, including government ministers and Zeroual's aides, are running for the National Assembly's 380 seats. Islamist parties are banned by the new constitution approved last November.
Zeroual warned people against what he called demagogic election promises.
"The economic reforms are necessary to ensure the future of our sons and our country," he said, adding that more reforms lay ahead including in the industrial sector.
Algeria's industrial output, excluding oil and gas, fell seven percent in 1996.
